extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society; natural philosophers, astronomers, botanists, and practical men (shipwrights, timber buyers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for conducting, reporting, and judging natural-philosophy observations and practical techniques (astronomical observations, timber-felling and bark-curing, botanical description, hydrologic reasoning) as communicated to the Royal Society in late 17th-century practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for felling timber (general seasonal rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the ancients advise the felling of timber for any sort of use before autumn at soonest; others, not till the trees have borne their fruit; others again not till mid-winter; not till November says Palladius; nay, not till the winter solstice, says Cato; and then too in the decrease or wane of the moon, between the 15th and 23d day of her age, says Vegetius; or rather, according to Columella, between the 20th and the new moon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: in winter the sap is at rest, pores are closed by cold air and the tree is consolidated, so timber felled late in the year will neither shrink, warp, cleave, nor decay for many years and will be 'tough as horn'. Citations to Theophrastus, Vegetius, Pliny, Vitruvius and others as supporting authorities. Implication: prefer felling oak (and other building timbers) very late in the year (November–mid-winter) for durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bark-off-in-spring, fell-in-winter (Staffordshire method)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of taking the bark off in the spring while the tree stands, leaving the tree standing all summer exposed to sun and wind, and felling it the following winter produces trunks so dried and hardened that the sappy part becomes as firm and durable as the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method yields timber that is close, substantial and durable—preferred for shipbuilding. Acknowledged downside: more troublesome and more costly than barking after felling. Legislative note: an Act (1 Jac. I, chap. 22) forbids felling for ordinary uses in certain months, but has an exception for ship timber, allowing winter felling. Procurement recommendation: officers may buy timber only under conditions that it be felled in winter after spring barking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid felling in spring (risks of putrefaction and shrinkage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Timber felled in spring, when trees are 'pregnant' and sap is up, retains juices in pores which putrify and breed worms; such timber is subject to rift, gape and significant shrinkage (example: a foot-square piece may shrink 1/8 inch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: timber felled in spring is pernicious for uses requiring strength (e.g., shipbuilding) and should be avoided. Historical authorities (Vegetius, Julius Caesar, Pliny) cited for performance differences between spring-felled and late-winter-felled timber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer timber from exposed sites for shipbuilding; avoid coppice/wood-grown trees
rubrics_metrics.description: Timber most exposed to cold winds or sun (open fields, parks, hedge-rows, forests with exposure) becomes harder and tougher; trees growing in shady, moist woods or coppices are less good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: for royal shipyards do not buy timber growing in woods or coppices; require timber from exposed situations and felled in winter (after spring barking). Rationale: exposure to sun/wind dries and hardens wood and yields better material for ships. Procurement officers should condition purchases accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile tanning legislation with best timber practice (procurement/legal exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an Act forbidding felling timber for ordinary uses between 1 April and 30 June for the sake of tanning (bark removal), but the author notes that barking in spring while the tree stands still permits felling in winter and thus does not defeat tanners' needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the law did not contemplate spring-on-tree barking; an exception for ship timber already exists. Practical policy: purchase contracts can require spring barking and winter felling so both tan supply and high-quality ship timber are secured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report astronomical observations with timed precision and observational context
rubrics_metrics.description: When recording an eclipse (example: lunar eclipse observed at Moscow), note precise local times of appearance/obscuration phases, the moon's altitude above horizon, instances of cloud cover, and what instrument was used (e.g., small telescope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowance: a not-fully-instructed observer may err by ~8–10 minutes in distinguishing penumbra from true shadow; such uncertainty should be allowed when comparing observations. Use simultaneous observations at different locations (Leipsic vs Moscow) and published ephemerides/tables (which 'never err sensibly in the continuance of eclipses') to compute differences of meridians/longitude. Example: use end-times of eclipse to determine longitudinal differences between places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish penumbra from umbra; report instrument limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers not sufficiently instructed may fail to distinguish penumbra (partial shadow) from true shadow (umbra), even when using a small telescope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring/evaluation note: allow a temporal allowance (several minutes) for such observational ambiguity; explicitly record whether penumbral phases were considered to avoid misinterpretation when comparing observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curing Pimenta (Jamaica pepper) fruit (post-harvest handling standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fruit is cured by pulling off twigs with unripe green fruit, separating fruit from twigs/leaves/ripe berries, exposing them to the sun spread thin on cloths, turning them now and then, and carefully avoiding the dews until they dry and change from green to brown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality indicators: smaller and more fragrant berries are accounted better. Practical tip: harvest practices (timing, separation, sun-drying, protection from dew) are critical to marketable product quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curing wild cinnamon (bark) for use
rubrics_metrics.description: The bark of the wild cinnamon tree is chiefly in use and is easily cured by cutting off the bark and suffering it to dry in the shade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical instruction: minimal processing—strip and shade-dry—yields the product used in plantations and for export.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological standard for explaining the circulation of sea vapours
rubrics_metrics.description: Use combined experimental measurement (quantity of water raised in vapour from the sea per day) and reasoned hypothesis about atmospheric behaviour to explain how vapour returns to the sea: by mountain condensation, dews/rains over ocean, river runoff, and local evaporation cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley's approach: demonstrate by experiment the amount of vapour produced, then use analogy (salts dissolved in warm water precipitating on cooling) and geographic/topographic reasoning (mountains acting like alembics distilling fresh water; the relation of ridge height/length to river magnitude) to argue that the net effect over long time is equilibrium between sea loss and return. Evaluation criterion: favor hypotheses that reconcile observed river sources, persistence of springs during drought, and experimental vapour data over theories like simple filtration of sea water through imagined earth passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary criteria for the theory of generation (ex animalculo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three things seem very probable: (1) that animals are ex animalculo; (2) that these animalcules are originally in semine marum, et non in foeminis; (3) that they can never come forward, nor be formed into animals of the respective kind, without the ova in foeminis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive evidence enumerated: (a) Malpighi's repeated observations of rudiments in the cicatricula of an egg before incubation; (b) the sudden appearance and displaying of all parts after incubation suggesting pre-existing rudiments rather than new formation from fluid; (c) microscopic observations (after 30–40 hours of incubation) showing early formation of head, eyes, vertebrae, heart and even pulse. Evaluation practice: weigh direct microscopic observation, timing of visible development, and comparative embryological accounts when adjudicating competing theories of generation (ex ovo vs ex animalculo).
